questions.q: What did the Ljung-Box(10) test results show for all five ARMA fits in this lesson?
options: All p-values were below 0.05, indicating significant leftover autocorrelation in every model
All p-values were well above 0.05, indicating no significant autocorrelation left in the residuals -- a clean pass
The Ljung-Box test could not be computed for any of the five assets
Only QRBT passed the Ljung-Box test
questions.explain: All five assets' Ljung-Box(10) p-values (0.774, 0.202, 0.506, 0.220, 0.877) were well above the 0.05 threshold, meaning none of the fitted ARMA models left significant autocorrelation behind in its residuals.

questions.q: COBM and PRAI were both fit with ARMA order (0, 0, 0) -- pure white noise. Why does the lesson say this is the expected, correct outcome rather than a bug?
options: Because ARIMA always returns (0,0,0) for assets starting with the letters C or P
Because the universe was simulated with GARCH dynamics only in variance, not in the mean, so there is no true mean-level autocorrelation for ARMA to detect
Because COBM and PRAI had zero trading volume in the simulation
Because (0,0,0) is always the best AIC choice regardless of the data
questions.explain: The simulation built GARCH structure into variance (volatility clustering), not into the mean of returns, so assets with no real mean-autocorrelation correctly came back as white noise under an AIC search -- this matches the data-generating process, not a modeling error.

questions.q: COBM's fitted GARCH persistence came back at 0.764, noticeably below its 0.96 simulation target. What does the lesson say this illustrates?
options: That the arch package cannot fit GARCH models correctly
That GARCH parameters, especially beta, are difficult to pin down precisely from a single ~1,000-day sample, even when the true data-generating process is known exactly
That COBM's true persistence was actually 0.764, not 0.96
That Materials-sector stocks never exhibit volatility clustering
questions.explain: Because the data was simulated, the true persistence (0.96) is known exactly -- the fitted value (0.764) being lower highlights genuine estimation uncertainty in GARCH fitting on a finite sample, not a flaw in the simulation or the package.

questions.q: Where did the largest discrepancy between the sample covariance matrix and the one-factor-model covariance matrix show up, and why?
options: On the diagonal, because the factor model cannot estimate any asset's own variance
Off-diagonal, between QRBT and COBM (a gap of about 34), reflecting that the sample covariance also picks up incidental correlation between idiosyncratic shocks that the factor model assumes away
There was no discrepancy anywhere between the two matrices
In the correlation of VANU with itself
questions.explain: Diagonal entries matched closely since they both use each asset's own residual plus factor variance, but the QRBT-COBM off-diagonal entry differed by about 34 (293.5 vs 327.8), illustrating the factor model's simplifying assumption that all co-movement runs through the single common factor.

questions.q: How closely did the OLS-estimated factor betas match the true betas used to simulate the universe in Lesson 33?
options: They were completely unrelated to the true betas
They tracked the true betas closely -- for example QRBT's estimated beta was 1.325 versus a true value of 1.30, and VANU's was 0.341 versus a true value of 0.35
All estimated betas came back negative
The estimated betas were exactly double the true betas in every case
questions.explain: Every estimated beta landed close to its corresponding true simulation value (e.g. QRBT 1.325 vs 1.30, HALC 1.123 vs 1.15, VANU 0.341 vs 0.35), confirming the OLS estimation procedure recovered the underlying factor structure well.
